target: AG1’s claim that a national Election Day holiday would give many voters scheduling flexibility by reducing work/school barriers.
objection: A federal holiday does not reliably create paid time off for private-sector workers, especially in retail and service jobs, so many low-income workers would still have to work on Election Day and would not actually get the scheduling flexibility AG1 claims.

target: AG1’s assumption that a holiday meaningfully removes the work-based barriers faced by low-income voters.
objection: If low-income workers still must work on Election Day, then the holiday does not substantially reduce the work-time barrier for the people most affected by it.

target: AG1’s broader argument that an Election Day holiday is a good turnout policy.
objection: A federal holiday would disadvantage low-income workers and is unlikely, by itself, to increase turnout meaningfully, so the policy is not effective enough to justify.

target: AG1’s claim that holiday status would reliably help low-income workers by giving them non-work time.
objection: Because private employers are not required to provide paid leave or close on federal holidays, many retail and service workplaces could remain open and still schedule workers, so the holiday would not reliably create non-work time for hourly workers.

target: AG1’s claim that a federal holiday would meaningfully reduce work-based voting barriers for low-income voters.
objection: Many low-income workers are concentrated in private retail and service jobs, and because those jobs may remain open on federal holidays, their work conflicts with voting would often persist.

target: AG1’s general policy justification for Election Day as a holiday.
objection: Research-based voting-access policy should be judged by how reliably it reduces barriers, and an election holiday by itself is unlikely to be an effective turnout strategy compared with other reforms.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday would reduce school-based and caregiving barriers for many voters, including low-income families.
objection: School closure does not necessarily remove caregiving burdens; low-income parents may still need to arrange substitute childcare, which can cost time and money and may even increase barriers.

target: AG1’s assumption that school closure meaningfully helps low-income voters who face work constraints.
objection: If a low-income voter’s main obstacle is inability to take time off from work, school closure does not create a usable voting window, so the holiday does not reliably improve access for them.

target: AG1’s overall claim that simply making Election Day a holiday is the best way to improve voting access.
objection: A holiday changes the calendar but does not directly guarantee time off or reduced wage loss for the voters most affected; more targeted reforms like employer time-off rules or other access reforms are more reliable.

target: AG2’s claim that a federal holiday would not reliably create scheduling flexibility for low-income workers because private employers may stay open.
objection: Even if federal law does not force private employers to give paid time off, businesses commonly reduce hours or close on federal holidays, which changes employees’ actual schedules and creates real non-work time windows.

target: AG2’s claim that a federal holiday would not meaningfully reduce work-based voting barriers.
objection: When workplaces reduce hours or close for a holiday, workday conflicts with voting time decrease, so the holiday does reduce the barrier and makes voting more accessible.

target: AG2’s conclusion that Election Day should not be a national holiday because the policy does not help enough.
objection: Because the holiday would reduce scheduling barriers, it would increase turnout and civic engagement, so the policy is beneficial rather than ineffective.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday would not reliably help hourly workers because employers are not required to pay them.
objection: In practice, many retail and service employers adjust hours or close on federal holidays, so hourly workers often do get actual non-work time rather than just a symbolic holiday label.

target: AG2’s claim that work-based voting costs would persist for many low-income workers even under a holiday.
objection: When employers reduce hours or close on Election Day, workers can vote without taking extra time that costs wages or scarce paid leave, so the holiday meaningfully reduces those costs.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday would not improve turnout enough to justify it.
objection: A national Election Day holiday would increase turnout and civic engagement by removing scheduling barriers, so the policy does improve participation.

target: AG2’s skepticism about the cultural value of a holiday.
objection: Making voting occur on a holiday elevates the importance of civic participation and democracy, turning voting into a celebration rather than a chore.

target: AG2’s implication that broad support and foreign precedent do not support the holiday idea.
objection: The fact that 71% of Democrats and 59% of Republicans support the measure, and that 27 of 36 OECD countries hold elections on weekends or holidays, shows broad bipartisan support and established international feasibility.

target: AG2’s claim that school closure does not help low-income voters because caregivers may still need to arrange substitute care.
objection: Even if some private employers remain open, school closure still gives caregivers and families more daytime flexibility to handle obligations like voting, so a holiday can reduce school- and caregiving-related barriers.

target: AG2’s claim that the lack of employer-mandated paid time off means low-income voters would get no meaningful relief.
objection: The objection assumes that only employer-paid leave matters, but a holiday can still create scheduling relief through school closure and reduced work obligations, which helps low-income voters even if not all employers close.
